# Graded Exercise Therapy for ME/CFS — Meta-Analysis Report

*A rapid, AI-assisted meta-analysis with source-verified extraction. Generated by the Metascience Observatory pipeline.*

## Objective

To estimate the effect of **graded exercise therapy (GET)** versus non-exercise control on **fatigue** and **physical function** in myalgic encephalomyelitis / chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), and to characterise **harms**. This is framed as a **methods/automation exercise** and an update lens rather than a replacement for the Cochrane review (Larun et al., last searched 2014): it incorporates newer pragmatic RCTs (GETSET 2017, MAGENTA 2024), foregrounds harms and diagnostic-criteria sensitivity (central to NICE's 2021 withdrawal of GET), and demonstrates an AI-extraction pipeline hardened by adversarial verification against source documents.

## Methods

### Eligibility (PICO)
- **Population:** adults or children with ME/CFS / chronic fatigue syndrome (any diagnostic criteria).
- **Intervention:** graded exercise therapy / graded activity as a distinct trial arm (including CBT+GET combined arms, flagged).
- **Comparator:** any non-exercise control (usual care / specialist medical care, waitlist, adaptive pacing (APT), CBT, relaxation).
- **Outcomes:** fatigue (Chalder Fatigue Scale / FSS), physical function (SF-36 physical function, 6-minute walk), and harms (serious adverse events / withdrawal due to worsening).
- **Design:** randomised controlled trials.

### Search & screening
Two search streams were unioned and de-duplicated: (1) a PubMed protocol search (154 records) and (2) a multi-database graded-exercise-tagged set from PubMed, OpenAlex, Europe PMC and Semantic Scholar (113 records) — **174 unique records** assessed. A GET-specific PICO screen (11 parallel AI screeners plus adjudication) excluded 149 (reviews/editorials 64; non-GET interventions — drug/supplement/acupuncture/mind-body 34; non-RCT 23; mechanistic/physiology-only 11; protocols 8; wrong population 6; conference abstracts 3), leaving **21 reports of 12 distinct trials**.

### Data extraction — AI extraction + adversarial verification + source recovery
Quantitative data were extracted from full text by an LLM (Claude Sonnet, via the pipeline's `9_extract_pass2` extractor). Each extraction was then **adversarially audited** by an independent LLM auditor against the source text. This caught a **critical, systematic failure**: GROBID PDF-to-text conversion had silently dropped the primary-outcome results tables in **7 of 11 trials — including PACE**, the largest and most influential trial, whose 52-week Chalder-fatigue and SF-36-PF data were entirely absent from the machine-readable text. Primary-outcome contrasts were therefore **recovered directly from the authoritative source** (publisher JATS-XML where available — e.g. PACE, GETSET — otherwise the original PDF tables), each with a verbatim evidence quote. A separate check confirmed **Powell 2001's** SF-36 PF is on the non-standard 10–30 subscale (not 0–100) and fatigue on the Chalder 0–11 bimodal scale, and that its dispersion figures are correct SDs back-converted from published 95% CIs — validating the use of **standardised** (not raw) mean differences.

### Statistical analysis
Standardised mean differences (**Hedges' g**) were computed from source-verified per-arm means/SDs and oriented so **positive favours GET**. Effects were pooled with **DerSimonian–Laird random effects** and **Hartung–Knapp–Sidik–Jonkman (HKSJ)** confidence intervals (better small-*k* coverage), with I², τ² and 95% prediction intervals. Pre-specified analyses: **subgroups** by diagnostic criteria (Oxford vs stricter/other) and age (adult vs paediatric); **sensitivity** by leave-one-out, DL-normal CI, and exclusion of the Powell outlier. Certainty was rated with a deterministic **GRADE** implementation. Serious-adverse-event / harm data were pooled as a **risk ratio** (log scale, 0.5 continuity correction for zero cells). Four included trials were held out of the primary pool: **Gordon 2010** (head-to-head exercise, no non-exercise control), **Núñez 2011** (combined CBT+GET, GET not isolable), and **Wearden 1998 / Wallman 2004** (between-group-only or SD-absent).

## Results

### Study flow
174 records screened → 149 excluded → **12 trials** included; **6** contribute to the fatigue pool, **6** to physical function, **7** to harms.

### Risk of bias
**All trials are at high risk of bias** for the primary self-reported outcomes: GET cannot be blinded, so participants, therapists and (usually) assessors are unmasked, and the co-primary outcomes (Chalder fatigue, SF-36 PF) are participant-rated — a structural performance/detection-bias problem for the entire evidence base. Allocation concealment was generally adequate (central randomisation).

### Fatigue (6 RCTs, n ≈ 860)
Pooled **SMD 0.74 (95% CI 0.15 to 1.34)**, I² = 86.6%, τ²-driven 95% prediction interval −0.69 to 2.18. **GRADE: very low** (downgraded for risk of bias and inconsistency ×2).

| Trial | Year | Criteria | SMD (95% CI) | Weight |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PACE (White) | 2011 | Oxford | 0.45 (0.23, 0.68) | 19.0% |
| GETSET (Clark) | 2017 | NICE | 0.52 (0.24, 0.81) | 18.4% |
| Ridsdale | 2012 | primary-care | 0.08 (−0.30, 0.47) | 17.2% |
| Powell | 2001 | Oxford | **1.72 (1.29, 2.15)** | 16.6% |
| Fulcher & White | 1997 | Oxford | 0.83 (0.30, 1.37) | 15.1% |
| Moss-Morris | 2005 | Fukuda | 1.00 (0.37, 1.63) | 13.7% |

- **Subgroups:** Oxford (k=3) SMD **0.99**; non-Oxford (k=3) SMD **0.48**.
- **Excluding the Powell outlier:** SMD falls to **0.51 (0.12, 0.89)** and heterogeneity roughly halves (I² 87% → 53%). Leave-one-out range 0.51–0.88.

### Physical function (6 RCTs)
Pooled **SMD 0.51 (95% CI −0.09 to 1.11)** — **confidence interval crosses the null** — I² = 88.7%, prediction interval −0.95 to 1.97. **GRADE: very low** (risk of bias, inconsistency ×2, imprecision).

| Trial | Year | Criteria | SMD (95% CI) | Weight |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PACE (White) | 2011 | Oxford | 0.27 (0.04, 0.49) | 18.6% |
| GETSET (Clark) | 2017 | NICE | 0.20 (−0.08, 0.48) | 18.1% |
| MAGENTA | 2024 | NICE/other | −0.08 (−0.36, 0.20) | 18.1% |
| Powell | 2001 | Oxford | **1.55 (1.12, 1.97)** | 16.4% |
| Fulcher & White | 1997 | Oxford | 0.68 (0.16, 1.21) | 15.0% |
| Moss-Morris | 2005 | Fukuda | 0.61 (0.00, 1.23) | 13.8% |

- **Subgroups:** Oxford (k=3) SMD **0.82**; non-Oxford (k=3) SMD **0.16** (near-null).
- **Excluding Powell:** SMD **0.26 (−0.10, 0.61)** — remains non-significant. Leave-one-out range 0.26–0.64.
- The three **large, rigorous pragmatic trials** (PACE, GETSET, MAGENTA) show **small-to-null** physical-function effects (0.27, 0.20, −0.08).

### Harms (7 RCTs)
Serious-adverse-event / harm-related-withdrawal **risk ratio 1.58 (95% CI 0.78 to 3.20)**, I² = 0% (harms counted as participants with ≥1 serious adverse event or harm-related withdrawal). The point estimate is **elevated but imprecise** and the CI includes 1; PACE is the largest contributor (RR 1.86, 95% CI 0.76–4.53). No trial demonstrated GET to be protective against harm.

## Discussion

The pooled effects are **in the same range as the Cochrane review** (Larun et al. reported ~SMD 0.66 for fatigue), but this analysis makes explicit **why the certainty is very low**:

1. **Effect size tracks methodological rigour and diagnostic breadth.** Large effects come almost entirely from **small, older, Oxford-criteria trials** (Powell, Fulcher & White, Moss-Morris); the **large pragmatic trials that used stricter criteria** (PACE, GETSET, MAGENTA) show modest-to-null effects, especially for physical function (SMD 0.16 in the non-Oxford subgroup). Oxford criteria do not require post-exertional malaise and admit patients with idiopathic chronic fatigue who may not have ME/CFS — the core of the **NICE 2021** rationale for withdrawing GET.
2. **Physical-function benefit is not robust.** The pooled SMD crosses the null and falls to ~0.26 once the Powell outlier is removed.
3. **A non-trivial harms signal** (RR ~1.6) is imprecise but points in the direction of increased harm, consistent with patient-reported deterioration that motivated the guideline change.
4. **Unblindable, self-reported outcomes** make the entire evidence base high risk of bias — no amount of pooling can repair this.

**Methods contribution.** The pipeline's value here was the **verification-and-recovery layer**: naïve AI extraction would have silently dropped PACE's primary outcomes (lost by GROBID), badly biasing the pool. Independent adversarial auditing detected this and every number in the primary analyses is now traceable to a verbatim source quote (`recovered_contrasts.json`).

## Limitations
- **Small evidence base** (6 trials per primary outcome) with very high heterogeneity; prediction intervals cross zero.
- **Screening and extraction were AI-driven** (single automated reviewer with adversarial audit) rather than dual independent human reviewers.
- **FINE (Wearden 2010, BMJ)** — a major pragmatic-rehabilitation trial — could not be included because its primary-outcome paper was absent from the search corpus (only its 2013 mediation paper was retrieved); its inclusion (favouring the null) would likely reduce the pooled effect.
- **Wearden 1998 and Wallman 2004** report only between-group differences / lack per-arm SDs and were held to sensitivity analyses; **Powell 2001** is patient *education* to encourage self-managed graded exercise, not supervised therapist-led GET.
- Harms definitions are heterogeneous across trials (serious adverse events vs harm-related withdrawal).

## Conclusion
Graded exercise therapy is associated with a **small-to-moderate reduction in fatigue** and a **non-robust, near-null effect on physical function** in ME/CFS, on **very-low-certainty** evidence. Apparent benefits are concentrated in **small, older, broad-criteria (Oxford) trials**; the largest and most rigorous trials show modest-to-null effects, and there is an **imprecise but elevated harms signal**. These findings are consistent with the 2021 NICE decision to stop recommending GET and underscore that the ME/CFS exercise-therapy evidence base is limited by unblindable interventions with self-reported outcomes.
